doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Audio clip: Shaw recording and Conniff's best arrangements
summary: After a clip of an Artie Shaw recording from 1940, Conniff names it and Harry James's 'September Song' as his two best arrangements, which he later re-recorded.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Let me play something for you here.
Would it be all right if I used one of these?
Does that ring a bell with you?
Yeah, that’s originally Artie Shaw, isn’t it?
Yeah. In 1940 we recorded that, yeah.
So at this point, you were still writing for the guys in the band, but it still had that very predominant rhythm thing happening, right up front.

Well it’s strange that you picked that particular recording out, because on that particular recording, you know, all through the years working with the bands, and I really started playing I guess, you play professionally when you get paid for a gig. And the first time I got paid for a gig it was in 1933 when I was in high school. And so all through the years, and I was writing at the same time. I must tell you sometime during the interview how I started writing. I got a little device called a “lightning arranger.” I paid a dollar for a mail order device and I wrote my first arrangement with a dollar mail order device. But anyway, you write yourself, don’t you? Yeah. Well you probably, I don’t know if you’re anything like me, I think out of every hundred arrangements I probably write, there’s one that I think really came off either recording or the way I wrote or everything. And this was one when I brought this in and heard this, and heard it performed, I thought, this is one of the best things I’ve ever done for coming together you know, for the whole, the routine, the whole thing. And I thought if I ever get my own group, I’m going to re- record that again. And I would say there were two that I did like that during my whole career with the big bands. The other one was Harry James’ “September Song.” That turned out great too. And both of those arrangements, you know I was trying to give it, as you probably do, all my best effort, you know, my best shot, and work a long time before I put any notes down. But those two really turned out. So I did re-record both of those. So you picked one that even though it was written with the older era of the guys in the band and Artie Shaw, the thought that went into it turned out, although it didn’t use the hit formula idea, the way all the elements came together was, I would say, even though it’s with a great jazz band, it’s commercial you know. People can understand it. They can hear the melody, they can feel the rhythm.
And they were still dancing to the music at that time.
And so it had that kind of — it was a touch of Latin beat in there too.
